concepts.title: Colonialism as a Structure and System
concepts.definition: Colonialism is the imposition of one country's rule over another territory. Under capitalism it worked far deeper than earlier empires: instead of merely skimming tribute off an untouched economy, it rewrote property law, dictated which crops were grown, reorganised manufacture and trade, entered the forests, and moved people across continents to serve metropolitan interests.
concepts.formula: colonial_rule = tribute_not_enough ; depth = laws + crops + manufacturing + forests + migration
concepts.key_idea: Pre-capitalist conquerors took a flow of surplus and left the base alone; British rule rebuilt production itself, so its effects still shape Indian institutions today.
concepts.textbook_ref: lesy201.txt, section 1.1 opening (Alavi and Shanin 1982), Box 1.1
question_patterns: in what way was british colonialism different from the tribute collection of pre-capitalist conquerors?

solution_steps.action: contrast tribute empires with capitalist colonialism
solution_steps.explain: earlier conquerors skimmed surplus the economy already produced; british rule changed land law, crop choices, manufacturing, forests and trade so as to feed british capitalism

solution_steps.action: check the unintended outcome
solution_steps.explain: western schooling introduced to staff the administration instead bred nationalist and anti-colonial consciousness

concepts.title: Capitalism and the Nation State as Modern Forms
concepts.definition: Capitalism is an economic arrangement in which private owners run production for profit inside a market, constantly expanding and innovating. Its matching political form is the nation state: a sovereign government over a defined territory whose people are citizens of one nation. Nationalism claims every people has the right to such self rule, which is precisely what colonial domination denied Indians.
concepts.formula: modern_pair = capitalism_economic + nation_state_political ; sovereignty = defined_territory + single_citizenship
concepts.key_idea: Colonialism contradicted its own ideals: Britain carried nationalist and democratic ideas to India while refusing Indians the sovereignty those ideas promised.
concepts.textbook_ref: lesy201.txt, section 1.1 closing passages on nation states and swaraj
question_patterns: define capitalism and explain why it is a dynamic and expanding system

solution_steps.action: match each modern form to its domain
solution_steps.explain: capitalism organises the economy around private ownership and profit in a market; the nation state concentrates sovereign power over a territory of citizens

solution_steps.action: test the contradiction
solution_steps.explain: nationalism holds that any people may exercise sovereign power, while colonial rule is rule by foreigners, so leaders demanded swaraj as a birthright and fought for political and economic freedom

concepts.title: Industrialisation: The Western Path and the Colonial Diversion
concepts.definition: Industrialisation is the shift of production to machines run on non-living energy such as steam or electricity, drawing most workers out of farming into factories, offices and shops. In Britain this ran together with city growth, but in colonial India the same british machinery ruined handicraft exports and pushed people back into agriculture instead.
concepts.formula: western_path = machines + city_growth ; colonial_path = handicraft_decline + shift_to_farming
concepts.key_idea: Manchester goods destroyed indian cotton and silk exports; surat and masulipatnam declined while bombay and madras grew, and court cities like murshidabad lost their artisans.
concepts.textbook_ref: lesy201.txt, section 1.2 The Colonial Experience, Box 1.2
question_patterns: define industrialisation and name the power resources it depends on

solution_steps.action: contrast the two directions of movement
solution_steps.explain: in britain machine production drew people into towns; in india cheap imports and new factories broke village industries, so labour drifted into agriculture

solution_steps.action: check which centres rose and fell
solution_steps.explain: handicraft export hubs and court cities declined as court demand and external markets collapsed; colonial port cities handling raw material exports expanded

concepts.title: Britain's Urban Transition 1800 to 1900
concepts.definition: Britain was the first society to turn from rural to mainly urban. Census style arithmetic turns that story into numbers: the percentage point rise in the town dwelling share, and the growth multiple by which london expanded across the nineteenth century.
concepts.formula: urban_rise = urban_share_1900 - urban_share_1800 ; london_multiple = london_1900 / london_1800
concepts.key_idea: A percentage point rise measures the change in a share, while a multiple compares two sizes directly by division.
question_patterns: in 1800 well under 20 per cent of britain's people lived in towns of more than 10000 inhabitants; by 1900 the figure was 74 per cent. calculate the percentage point rise
london held about 1.1 million people in 1800 and over 7 million by 1900. how many times did the city multiply?

compute the growth multiple of london's population between 1800 and 1900

solution_steps.action: subtract the early share from the later share
solution_steps.explain: the difference of two census shares gives the rise in percentage points

solution_steps.action: divide the rise by the number of decades
solution_steps.explain: spreading the century of change over ten decades gives the average pace

solution_steps.action: divide the later city size by the earlier size
solution_steps.explain: the ratio of the two populations is the growth multiple

concepts.title: Colonial Port Cities as Core-Periphery Links
concepts.definition: Colonial cities sat on the coast to serve empire trade: primary commodities flowed out through mumbai, kolkata and chennai, and british manufactures flowed cheaply in. They were the visible gateways joining the capitalist core in britain to the colonised periphery in india.
concepts.formula: city_role = export_raw_materials + import_manufactures ; link = core_britain + periphery_india
concepts.key_idea: By 1900 over three quarters of india's raw cotton moved through bombay; calcutta shipped jute while madras sent coffee, sugar, indigo dyes and cotton.
concepts.textbook_ref: lesy201.txt, section 1.2 Cities had a key role in the economic system of empires; Activity 1.1
question_patterns: why were the chief colonial cities all located on the coast?

solution_steps.action: check the direction of trade
solution_steps.explain: raw materials left for britain through the ports and cheap manufactured goods entered through the same gateways

solution_steps.action: check the redevelopment evidence
solution_steps.explain: bombay was planned and redeveloped so that by 1900 over three quarters of india's raw cotton shipped through it; kolkata began from three leased villages and fort william

concepts.title: Tea Plantation Workforce Arithmetic 1903
concepts.definition: Assam's tea gardens ran on workers imported from distant provinces, recruited through contractors, fraud and penal laws. The 1903 payroll lists permanent and temporary employees; adding the two gives the industry's total strength, and division turns each category into a share of the workforce.
concepts.formula: total_workforce = permanent_workers + temporary_workers ; temporary_share = temporary_workers / total_workforce * 100
concepts.key_idea: A two category payroll becomes shares by one addition and one part-whole division scaled by a hundred.
concepts.textbook_ref: lesy201.txt, Box 1.5 How were labourers recruited (1903 employment figures)
question_patterns: in 1903 the tea industry employed 479000 permanent and 93000 temporary employees. find the total workforce

solution_steps.action: add the two payroll categories
solution_steps.explain: permanent plus temporary employees give the total employed

solution_steps.action: divide the temporary count by the total and scale
solution_steps.explain: part over whole times a hundred gives the temporary share

solution_steps.action: subtract the temporary share from a hundred
solution_steps.explain: the complement is the permanent share

concepts.title: M S A Rao's Three Types of Urban Impact on Villages
concepts.definition: Rao sorts village-urban contact into three situations: villagers migrating singly to distant cities while families stay behind in the natal village; villages uprooted or partly acquired when an industrial town such as bhilai rises nearby; and villages absorbed, or their land taken, as a metropolis expands.
concepts.key_idea: The nature of urban influence depends on the kind of relation a village has with a city or town - how distant it is and what sort of centre it is.
question_patterns: describe the three situations of urban impact on villages identified by m s a rao

solution_steps.action: list the three situations
solution_steps.explain: employment migration to far-off cities, displacement and land acquisition near new industrial towns, and absorption or land take-over under expanding metropolises

solution_steps.action: check the village evidence
solution_steps.explain: madhopur migrants concentrate in bombay and calcutta, most remit money and visit often; gujarat villagers abroad built houses, bought land and funded schools and trusts

worked_examples.q: M.S.A. Rao sorts village-urban contact into how many situations: three or thirty?

concepts.title: Village Migration Shares from Household Counts
concepts.definition: Survey counts become shares by division: households with migrants over all households gives the migration rate, its complement gives the stayers, and the stayers' count follows from the share.
concepts.key_idea: Every part-whole percentage is one division scaled by a hundred, and its complement falls out by subtraction.
concepts.textbook_ref: lesy201.txt, Box 1.7 Madhopur figures (77 of 298 households, 75 per cent remit, 83 per cent visit)
question_patterns: in madhopur 77 out of 298 households have migrants. what percentage of households does migration touch?

83 per cent of the migrants visit the village at least once in two years. what share visit less often?

solution_steps.action: divide migrant households by all households and scale
solution_steps.explain: the part-whole ratio times a hundred is the migration share

solution_steps.action: subtract from a hundred
solution_steps.explain: the complement is the staying share

solution_steps.action: apply the staying share to the household total
solution_steps.explain: share times total over a hundred returns the count of non-migrant households

worked_examples.q: Migrant households over all households gives the migration what: rate or tax?

concepts.title: Urban India 1951 to 2011: Shares, Totals and Growth
concepts.definition: Census tables report the urban percentage and the urban population in millions. Dividing one by the other recovers the national total, a subtraction across the sixty years gives overall growth, and the ratio of town counts shows how the urban system multiplied - even while the decennial growth rate trended down.
concepts.formula: total_pop = urban_pop / (urban_share / 100) ; overall_growth = (urban_2011 - urban_1951) / urban_1951 * 100 ; town_multiple = towns_2011 / towns_1951
concepts.key_idea: The urban share climbed from about 17 to 31 per cent while the decennial growth rate fell from 41.42 to 31.80, and for the first time urban areas added more people than rural ones.
concepts.textbook_ref: lesy201.txt, urban population charts and 1951-2011 passage before the Conclusion
question_patterns: in 2011, 377.10 million people formed 31.16 per cent of india's population. estimate the total population of india

solution_steps.action: divide the urban population by its share
solution_steps.explain: urban pop divided by the urban fraction recovers the national total

solution_steps.action: compare the two census urban populations
solution_steps.explain: increase over the base, scaled by a hundred, is the overall growth rate

solution_steps.action: divide the later town count by the earlier
solution_steps.explain: the ratio of town counts is the multiplication factor of the urban system
